steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a paper on unsupervised bilingual lexicon induction for extremely low-resource languages that are closely related to a high-resource one, focusing on Indic languages related to Hindi. Cover motivation, why current methods fail, our method, evaluation setup and releases, and broader relevance.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Why bilingual lexicons matter
- Limits of existing BLI methods for low-resource languages
- Our setting: low-resource Indic languages close to Hindi
- Our method
- Evaluation, control experiments and released resources
- Relevance beyond the Indic continuum

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Bilingual lexicons: basic resource; dictionary building, language learning; seeds for NLP: parsing, word-to-word and unsupervised MT (refs)
- Existing BLI
  - interest in unsupervised / minimally supervised BLI
  - rely on aligning monolingual embedding spaces (assumed good) and/or bilingual supervision (several refs)
  - extremely LRLs / dialects: poor embeddings, little data -> very low / near-zero performance (refs)
- Setting: under-researched Indic continuum (Section 2)
  - five languages: Bhojpuri (bho), Magahi (mag), Awadhi (awa), Maithili (mai), Braj (bra); close to Hindi
  - <5M tokens monolingual data; few embeddings, little evaluation data
  - SOTA alignment methods do poorly; new method much better; also produce resources
- Method
  - extremely LRLs overlapping with closely related HRL
  - HRL MLM e.g. monolingual BERT available; some monolingual LRL sentences w/ unknown words
  - iterative: HRL MLM over LRL sentences -> translation equivalents; replace learnt words with HRL equivalents (Section 4)
- Evaluation and release
  - no gold lexicons -> silver lexicons for Bhojpuri, Magahi from parallel data (none for Awadhi, Maithili, Braj)
  - controls: Marathi, Nepali (medium-resource, more distant, gold lexicons)
  - SOTA unsuitable for low-resource dialects; imbalance-aware methods better
  - release code, generated lexicons (first public except Bhojpuri), silver lexicons (Section 7)
- Broader relevance
  - 40+ resource-scarce Indic languages, other Indian languages
  - one high/medium resource standard dialect + related dialects, same script, w/ or w/o orthographic standard
  - e.g. Arabic continuum, Turkic continuum, German dialects

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Bilingual lexicons are a basic resource with many uses, both on their own, for dictionary building and language learning, and as seeds for solving other problems in natural language processing (NLP), like parsing and word-to-word and unsupervised machine translation.

There is growing interest in unsupervised or minimally supervised bilingual lexicon induction (BLI), but existing methods often rely on aligning monolingual word embedding spaces, which are assumed to be of good quality for both languages, and/or on bilingual supervision. But extremely low-resource languages (LRLs) and dialects often don't have good quality embeddings because they have limited monolingual data, and this leads to very low or near-zero performance of alignment-based methods for these languages.

This is the case for the Indic language continuum, which is under-researched and which is the focus of this article (Section 2 describes the linguistic setup in India that motivates our work). We work with five Indic languages that are extremely low-resourced, Bhojpuri (bho), Magahi (mag), Awadhi (awa), Maithili (mai), and Braj (bra). They are closely related to Hindi, which has more resources, and they have extremely limited resources in terms of training data (<5M tokens of monolingual data) and embeddings, and even evaluation data. We show that state-of-the-art alignment-based methods do poorly in these settings, and we introduce a new method for unsupervised BLI that does much better. We want to design methods that work well in typical data-scarce conditions, and also to generate resources for more work in these languages.

Evaluation and releases:
- no gold lexicons for target languages (common for extremely LRLs) -> silver lexicons for Bhojpuri and Magahi from parallel data; no parallel data for Awadhi, Maithili, Braj
- control experiments: Marathi and Nepali, medium-resource, more distantly related to Hindi, gold lexicons available; canonical methods vs ours
- current SOTA not suitable for low-resourced dialects; methods accounting for data imbalance (like ours) may do better
- release: code, generated lexicons (first public for all except Bhojpuri), silver lexicons for Bhojpuri and Magahi (Section 7)

Broader relevance:
- 40+ resource-scarce Indic languages, other Indian languages
- other systems: one high-or-medium resource language (standard dialect) + closely related dialects (lexical, morphological, syntactic variation), same script, with/without orthographic standardization
- e.g. Arabic continuum, Turkic continuum, German dialects

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Bilingual lexicons are a basic resource with many uses, both on their own, for dictionary building and language learning, and as seeds for solving other problems in natural language processing (NLP), like parsing and word-to-word and unsupervised machine translation.

There is growing interest in unsupervised or minimally supervised bilingual lexicon induction (BLI), but existing methods often rely on aligning monolingual word embedding spaces, which are assumed to be of good quality for both languages, and/or on bilingual supervision. But extremely low-resource languages (LRLs) and dialects often don't have good quality embeddings because they have limited monolingual data, and this leads to very low or near-zero performance of alignment-based methods for these languages.

This is the case for the Indic language continuum, which is under-researched and which is the focus of this article (Section 2 describes the linguistic setup in India that motivates our work). We work with five Indic languages that are extremely low-resourced, Bhojpuri (bho), Magahi (mag), Awadhi (awa), Maithili (mai), and Braj (bra). They are closely related to Hindi, which has more resources, and they have extremely limited resources in terms of training data (<5M tokens of monolingual data) and embeddings, and even evaluation data. We show that state-of-the-art alignment-based methods do poorly in these settings, and we introduce a new method for unsupervised BLI that does much better. We want to design methods that work well in typical data-scarce conditions, and also to generate resources for more work in these languages.

Our main contribution is a new unsupervised BLI method for the typical scenario of the LRLs of the Indic continuum, i.e. extremely LRLs that overlap significantly with a closely related HRL. We assume that a masked language model (MLM) like monolingual BERT is available for the HRL, and that we have some monolingual LRL sentences with unknown words. The method builds a lexicon iteratively. It uses the HRL MLM over LRL sentences to extract translation equivalents, and it replaces learnt words in the LRL sentences with their HRL equivalents so that the HRL MLM can handle them more easily for future unknown words (see Section 4).

There are no existing gold lexicons for our target languages (which happens a lot for extremely LRLs), so we create silver lexicons for Bhojpuri and Magahi from parallel data, which unfortunately is not available for Awadhi, Maithili, and Braj. We also do control experiments on Marathi and Nepali, two medium-resource languages that are more distantly related to Hindi and have gold lexicons, and we discuss how canonical methods and our method perform on these languages, which shows which strategies fit language pairs with different amounts of resources. Our experiments show that current state-of-the-art methods are not suitable for low-resourced dialects, and that methods that take the data imbalance in the language pair into account, like ours, may work better. We release our code, the lexicons we generated for all languages (as far as we know the first to be publicly released for all languages except Bhojpuri), and the silver evaluation lexicons we created for Bhojpuri and Magahi. Section 7 gives details of the released lexicons.

Our motivation and method are relevant for the 40+ resource-scarce languages of the Indic language family and other Indian languages, but also for other linguistic systems in a similar situation, i.e. with one high-or-medium resource language (usually a standard dialect) and several closely related dialects with lexical, morphological, and syntactic variation, written in the same script with or without orthographic standardization. For example, the Arabic continuum, the Turkic language continuum, and the German dialect system fit this setup.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Bilingual lexicons are a basic resource with varied uses, both in themselves, for dictionary building and language learning, and as seeds for solving other problems in natural language processing (NLP), such as parsing [1,2] and word-to-word and unsupervised machine translation [3,4].

While there is growing interest in unsupervised or minimally supervised bilingual lexicon induction (BLI), existing methods often depend on aligning monolingual word embedding spaces, assumed to be of good quality for both languages, and/or on bilingual supervision [5,6,7,8,9,10]. However, extremely low-resource languages (LRLs) and dialects often lack good quality embeddings because of limited monolingual data, which leads to very low or near-zero performance of alignment-based methods for these languages [11,12].

This is the case for the under-researched Indic language continuum, the focus of this article (see Section 2 for a description of the linguistic setup in India that motivates our work). We work with five extremely low-resourced Indic languages, Bhojpuri (bho), Magahi (mag), Awadhi (awa), Maithili (mai), and Braj (bra), which are closely related to higher-resourced Hindi and have extremely limited resources in terms of training data (<5M tokens of monolingual data), embeddings, and even evaluation data. We demonstrate that state-of-the-art, alignment-based methods perform poorly in these settings, and introduce a new unsupervised BLI method that performs much better. We aim to design methods that work well in characteristic data-scarce conditions, as well as to generate resources for further work in these languages.

Our main contribution is a novel unsupervised BLI method addressing the typical scenario of the LRLs of the Indic continuum, i.e. extremely LRLs that share significant overlap with a closely related HRL. We suppose that a masked language model (MLM) such as monolingual BERT [13] is available for the HRL and that we have some monolingual LRL sentences containing unknown words. The method builds a lexicon iteratively, using the HRL MLM over LRL sentences to extract translation equivalents and replacing learnt words in LRL sentences with HRL equivalents to make them more tractable for the HRL MLM for future unknown words (see Section 4).

Given the lack of existing gold lexicons for our target languages (a frequent scenario for extremely LRLs), we create silver lexicons for Bhojpuri and Magahi from parallel data, which is unfortunately unavailable for Awadhi, Maithili, and Braj. We also perform control experiments on Marathi and Nepali, two medium-resource languages more distantly related to Hindi with available gold lexicons, and discuss how canonical methods and our proposed method perform on these languages, shedding light on which strategies are appropriate for differently-resourced language pairs. Our experiments indicate that current state-of-the-art methods are not suitable for low-resourced dialects, and that methods that account for the data imbalance in the language pair, such as ours, may be more successful. We release our code, our generated lexicons for all languages (to our knowledge the first to be publicly released for all languages except Bhojpuri), and our silver evaluation lexicons for Bhojpuri and Magahi. Details of our released lexicons are given in Section 7.

Our motivation and method, while relevant to the 40+ resource-scarce languages of the Indic language family and other Indian languages, also apply to other linguistic systems in similar circumstances, i.e. with a single high-or-medium resource language (usually a standard dialect) and several closely related dialects with lexical, morphological, and syntactic variation, written in the same script with or without orthographic standardization. Examples of this setup are the Arabic continuum, the Turkic language continuum, and the German dialect system.
